title: Variables and print
summary: Store values under names and show them on screen.
intro:
A **variable** is a name that points at a value, like a label on a box. You make one by writing the name, then `=`, then the value. Read `=` as "gets": `score = 10` means "score gets 10".

To see a value on screen you use `print(...)`. In this lesson you will make a few variables, print them, change one, and watch the boxes on the right change as each line runs.

links.title: Python tutorial: numbers and variables (the = sign)
Python tutorial: text, and how print() shows it

lines.explain: Makes a new variable called **player** and puts the text `"Maya"` in it. The quotes tell Python this is text (a **str**, short for string). The quotes are not part of the value.
lines.task: Store the text Maya in a variable called player.

lines.explain: Makes a second variable, **score**, holding the whole number 10. Numbers have no quotes. Python calls whole numbers **int**.
lines.task: Store the number 10 in a variable called score.

lines.explain: `print` shows a value in the output. Python looks inside **player**, finds `"Maya"`, and prints it without the quotes. The variable itself does not change.
Same idea with a number. Python looks up **score** and prints 10.
You can give `print` several values separated by commas. It shows them in order with one space between each. Here two values come from variables and two are plain text.
lines.task: Print player, the word has, score and the word points in one print.

lines.explain: Assigning to a name that already exists **replaces** its value. The box now holds 25 and the old 10 is gone. Look for the "was 10" note in the panel.
The same kind of print as before, but `score` now gives 25. A variable always gives its **current** value at the moment the line runs.
lines.task: Print player, the words now has, score and the word points.

lines.explain: Makes **winner** point at the same value that **player** has right now, which is `"Maya"`. No quotes around `player`, so Python uses the variable, not the word.
lines.task: Make a variable called winner that gets the value of player.

lines.explain: Prints some fixed text and then the value inside **winner**. The text in quotes is printed exactly as written.
lines.task: Print the text Winner: followed by the value of winner.

quiz.q: After `score = 10` and then `score = 25`, what is stored in score?
quiz.why: A new assignment replaces the old value. A variable holds one value at a time.

quiz.q: In this lesson player holds "Maya". What does `print("player")` show?
quiz.why: The quotes make it plain text, so Python prints the word player instead of looking up the variable.
print puts one space between the values and leaves out the quotes.

quiz.q: These lines run in order: `x = 4`, then `y = x`, then `x = 3`. What is in y?
quiz.why: `y = x` gives y the value x had at that moment, 4. Changing x later does not touch y.

quiz.q: Which line gives an error if it is the very first line of a program?
quiz.why: total does not exist yet. A name must get a value before you can use it.
